Text:
Perform a neurologic assessment anytime a patient shows one of six trigger presentations. Four are ongoing states:

{{c1::changes in mental status}}

{{c1::stupor}}

{{c1::drowsiness}}

{{c1::dizziness}}
Back Extra:
Why: the assessment can begin hands-off — simply talking with the patient during the primary assessment already tests mental status.

Roster: changes in mental status · stupor · drowsiness · dizziness · possible head injury · syncope

Text:
Perform a neurologic assessment anytime a patient shows one of six trigger presentations. Two are discrete events:

{{c1::a possible head injury}}

{{c1::syncope}}
Back Extra:
Cue: "anytime you are confronted with" one of the six — syncope still counts even after the patient seems fully recovered.

Roster: changes in mental status · stupor · drowsiness · dizziness · possible head injury · syncope

Text: A man briefly fainted at church; by the time you arrive he is awake, oriented, and joking. His syncope alone still calls for a {{c1::neurologic::assessment type}} assessment.
Back Extra:
Why: syncope is one of the six standing triggers — a normal-looking recovery does not remove it.

Cue: start simple — talking, asking questions, and getting an appropriate reply already begins the assessment.

Text: The diameter and reactivity to light of a patient's pupils can reflect the status of the {{c1::brain::organ}} — its perfusion, oxygenation, and overall condition.
Back Extra: Why: pupil size is set from inside the skull by continuous automatic commands, so an organ in trouble up there can show itself in the eyes.

Text:
A healthy patient's pupils adjust their size to the available light:

In normal room light → {{c1::about midsize::size}}

With less light → {{c1::dilate::dilate/constrict}}

With a bright light shined near the eye → {{c1::constrict::dilate/constrict}}

In the absence of light → {{c1::fully relaxed and dilated::dilated/constricted}}
Back Extra:
Why: dilation lets more light into the eye — and normally pupil size changes instantly with any change in light level.

Pitfall: some patients' pupils do not react properly because of eye surgery or other conditions — confirm with the patient or family before reading meaning into it.

Text: When a brighter light is introduced into one eye only, {{c1::both::one/both}} pupils should constrict {{c1::equally::equally/unequally}}.
Back Extra: Why: the brain sets the two pupils to the appropriate size for the pupil receiving the most light.

Text: Pupil size is regulated by continuous motor commands that the brain automatically sends through the {{c1::oculomotor::cranial nerve}} nerves to each eye, constricting both pupils to the same appropriate size.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: each eye first sends sensory signals to the brain reporting its light level; the oculomotor commands are the brain's motor reply to each eye.

Cue: oculo- (eye) + motor (movement command) — the name says exactly what the nerves carry.

Text: You shine a penlight into a patient's right eye and watch her left pupil constrict as well. The motor command that reached that left eye traveled from the brain through the {{c1::oculomotor::cranial nerve}} nerves.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the light level travels TO the brain as sensory signals from each eye; the constriction order travels FROM the brain through the oculomotor nerves.

Cue: light in one eye sizes both pupils — the brain commands each eye together.

Text: {{c1::Anisocoria::pupil term}} is {{c2::normally unequal pupils}}, found in a small number of patients.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: unequal pupils count as "normal for the patient" only if the patient or a family member can confirm it — otherwise presume altered brain function from CNS depression or injury.

Parts: an- (not) + iso- (equal) + cor- (pupil) — pupils not equal.

Text:
Of the five abnormal pupil findings that indicate altered brain function, three are ways the reaction to light goes wrong:

{{c1::become fixed — no reaction at all (whether dilated or constricted)}}

{{c1::react backward — dilate when a bright light is introduced, constrict when it is removed}}

{{c1::react sluggishly instead of briskly}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: before calling a response abnormal, ask about eye surgery or other conditions that make odd pupils normal for this patient.

Roster: fixed (no reaction) · backward (dilate with light) · sluggish · unequal in size · unequal when light is introduced into or removed from one eye

Text: Two of the five abnormal pupil findings are not about how the pupils react — pupils that become {{c1::unequal in size::finding}}, at rest or {{c1::when a bright light is introduced into or removed from one eye::triggering moment}}, also indicate altered brain function.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a small number of patients have anisocoria — normally unequal pupils; inequality is presumed abnormal only when no one can confirm it as the patient's baseline.

Roster: fixed (no reaction) · backward (dilate with light) · sluggish · unequal in size · unequal when light is introduced into or removed from one eye

Text:
Causes of depressed brain function — the state abnormal pupils can reveal — include three structural ones:

{{c1::injury of the brain or brainstem}}

{{c1::trauma or stroke}}

{{c1::a brain tumor}}
Back Extra:
Cue: "some of the causes include" — an open set; these named ones are the classics, not an exhaustive list.

Roster: injury of the brain or brainstem · trauma or stroke · brain tumor · inadequate oxygenation or perfusion · drugs or toxins (CNS depressants)

Text:
Causes of depressed brain function — the state abnormal pupils can reveal — include two nonstructural ones:

{{c1::inadequate oxygenation or perfusion}}

{{c1::drugs or toxins (central nervous system depressants)}}
Back Extra:
Why: the brain fails without oxygen and blood flow even when nothing is structurally wrong — and CNS depressants turn it down chemically.

Roster: injury of the brain or brainstem · trauma or stroke · brain tumor · inadequate oxygenation or perfusion · drugs or toxins (CNS depressants)

Text:
In pupil assessment, the mnemonic PEARRL stands for:

{{c1::Pupils::P}}

{{c1::Equal::E}}

{{c1::And::A}}

{{c1::Round::R}}

{{c1::Regular in size::R}}

{{c1::React to Light::L}}
Back Extra: Cue: the two R's are different checks — Round is the shape, Regular in size is the size; the A is just "And."

visual_source.note: letter-by-letter expansion table read from render

Text: When a patient's pupil check is entirely normal, you can report it with the single mnemonic — "Pupils = {{c1::PEARRL}}" — while any abnormal finding must instead be {{c2::described using the longer form}}.
Back Extra: Ex: abnormal long form — "Pupils are equal and round, the left pupil is fixed and dilated, the right pupil is regular in size and reacts to light."

visual_source.note: report sentence and long-form example read from render

Text: After a fall, an older patient's pupils react sluggishly to your penlight and the left is larger than the right. No one can confirm a preexisting eye condition, so you should presume the abnormal response indicates {{c1::altered brain function (from CNS depression or injury)::significance}}.
Back Extra:
Why: pupil size is driven by the brain, so an unexplained abnormal response is treated as a brain problem until proven otherwise.

Cue: "normal for the patient" only counts when the patient or family can confirm it.
